item.title: Shame Kept Me Sick. Remorse Turned Me Outward.
item.description:
Shame

Shame Kept Me Sick. Remorse Turned Me Outward.

Personal Perspective: Shame asks what I am. Remorse asks what I did to you.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Shame ("I am bad") drives concealment; remorse ("I did harm") turns you outward toward repair.
  • Without insight into an illness, shame becomes the only available account of your own wreckage.
  • Sobriety alone did not free me; the insight that remorse opened, and the purpose it gave me, did.
  • Real repair moves the self out of the center: from "What kind of person am I?" to "What do I owe?"
Source: Feyza Yıldırım/Pexels

For nearly a decade, I was consumed by a shame I could not name and so could not master. I understand now that it was the shame of a sick man who did not know he was sick. I knew only its crushing weight, never its origin, and a grief whose source you cannot find is a grief you cannot answer.

So I did what people do with a feeling when it haunts them: I fled it. I drank in parking lots, stealing small sips until the dread dissipated. I smoked weed to quiet the nights the drinking could not reach. I hid my doctorate beneath a grocery-store apron; for a time, a supermarket felt like the only future I deserved. For those years the substances, not I, authored my life; I handed them the pen, having no ability to hold it.

The shame kept telling me that I was, at my core, a bad man. Not just that I had done bad things, but that I was fundamentally beyond redemption. I mistook that verdict for conscience. But it was conscience’s shadow: a thing that wore its face and did the inverse of its work.

Researchers who study these emotions distinguish shame from guilt, and the difference is the difference between sinking and swimming. In June Tangney’s account, shame latches on to the self and instills a moral message: I am bad. Guilt, in contrast, attaches to an act: I did something bad. Shame contaminates the essence of you, and its every instinct is to conceal. Guilt focuses on the wrong done and moves, however haltingly, toward repair.

For years, I fed the shame and starved the guilt, and my self-loathing, a punishment I inflicted nightly, resolved absolutely nothing. A man drowning in shame cannot face anyone he has wronged. He has only found a deeper way to drown in himself.

But I had wronged people. Under the spell of a manic episode I could not see was an illness, I sent terrorizing messages to colleagues and, worse, to the family and friends whose love I most needed. That harm is not what this essay is about; it is about what facing it made possible.

Without an appreciation of my sickness, the only account of my wreckage left standing was that, deep down, I was a bad person. The true agony of shame was its role in filling the space where insight should have been.

What Loosened the Grip

Jail and the psychiatric hospital took the bottle and the pipe from my hand. Sobriety came to me as a godsend, and it has held ever since, nearly two years now. But getting the substances out of my body only cleared space to reckon with the harder question: whether I could look at my shadow in the mirror, to bear to understand what had happened to me.

Insight arrived slowly, and, at first, alone. Reading Bessel van der Kolk in my cell, I found language for it: a person is made of parts—distinct selves, some tender, some capable of great damage. To keep them hidden, he warns, is to stay “at war with yourself.” I had long been at war with myself, cutting away the parts I could not tolerate. The work asked the opposite: to look at the sick self who had done the damage and grant that he too was mine—mine, and ill, and, through the light of self-knowledge, pushed into the penumbra of my psyche.

But insight alone was not enough. What made the transformation possible was connection and love: the mother I had wounded, who loved me anyway, and a few others, like my brother Cory, who would not give up on me. Held by them, I could look at what I had done without turning away.

My recovery did not follow a tidy trajectory. Shame did not lead to freedom directly. It led to remorse, and remorse, by turning me outward, led in turn to a fierce curiosity about my own illness—a need to understand the nature and origins of my madness so I might do whatever could be done to master it. That curiosity allowed me to make sense of the sickness behind my actions. Only once I could grasp it could I own it, and that ownership is what brought about a reconciliation with my mother and family. Armed with insight, I resolved to share my story with others—a vision of advocacy and purpose that set me free.

Source: Tony Frost/Unsplash

The Self Leaves the Center

Each turn, I see now, arrived as a question with a distinct premise. For years, shame asked only one: What kind of person am I? Remorse asked a better one: What did I do to you? Insight asked the question that finally explained me to myself: What happened inside me that made this possible? And responsibility asked the last and most useful of all: What must I do now?

Notice what happens to the ego across those four questions. The self, which shame had cemented to the dead center of everything, dissolves from the moral equation. By the end, the question is no longer what I am; it is what I owe. The answer starts close to home, in the prosaic work of staying well, then radiates outward. Part of that debt is the act of writing: telling the truth, and arguing for what might have spared me and might spare someone else. Insight offered to patients rather than withheld. Families let back into the room. Care built on connection and love instead of control.

Viktor Frankl wrote that suffering “ceases to be suffering at the moment it finds a meaning.” My pain still hurts, at times. But it stopped being only wreckage the moment it fastened to something larger than myself: the next person it might spare.

I used to believe the illness had ruined me. I have come to believe it broke a sealed man open, and that what climbed out was someone who could finally ask the thorny questions and live inside the messy answers: not innocent, not a victim, not condemned to repeat the past, but a man who can look at his own shadow in the mirror and who is responsible and connected to others. That is the only ground on which an honest life can be built.

item.title: The Thoughts Mothers Are Afraid to Tell You About
item.description:
Postpartum Depression

The Thoughts Mothers Are Afraid to Tell You About

Mothers need a safe place to tell the truth about postpartum mental illness.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • The Lindsay Clancy trial has renewed attention to postpartum mental illness and psychiatric care.
  • Postpartum depression, anxiety, intrusive thoughts, and psychosis are distinct conditions.
  • A frightening thought can require attention without defining a mother’s character or intent.
  • Fear of judgment or separation can make mothers afraid to disclose frightening thoughts.
It gets better.
Source: Loren Kleinman

As the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy unfolds in Massachusetts, I keep thinking about a journal I wrote seven years ago.

Clancy is on trial for killing her three young children in 2023. Her defense argues that she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and was not criminally responsible. Prosecutors dispute that account.

I don't know what happened inside Lindsay Clancy's mind. Her experience is not mine, and postpartum depression, anxiety, intrusive thoughts, and postpartum psychosis should not be treated as interchangeable.

But I know what happened inside my mind, and some of it still scares me to read: I want to leave. I don't want to be a mother. She was a mistake. And then sometimes, only hours later: I loved being her mother this afternoon.

I could love my daughter and want to escape motherhood. I could desperately miss her when someone else cared for her and simultaneously fantasize about being somewhere no one needed me. I could smell the top of her head after her bath and wish I could breathe her whole body into mine.

And I could wonder whether someone else should be her mother.

For a long time, I thought those thoughts told me something terrible about who I was. Eventually, I learned something that changed my recovery: A thought is not necessarily an intention.

But first I had to become willing to tell someone what I was thinking.

When Mothers Are Afraid to Tell the Truth

The Clancy trial has included testimony about psychiatric treatment, insomnia, depression, anxiety, suicidal thinking, medications, and intrusive thoughts.

Those words are difficult for me to read. Not because I believe my experience explains hers. What feels familiar is the terror of your own mind.

I remember sitting in therapy trying to calculate how much truth I could safely tell. I had been hospitalized and separated from my daughter. Medical professionals had raised the possibility of child protective services. So I started editing myself. Which thoughts could I admit? Which might send me back to the hospital? Which might make someone decide I shouldn't be around Lily?

Eventually I wrote something in my journal that frightens me now: Joe thinks I'm recovering but I'm good at hiding my truth.

A mental health system cannot treat what a patient is too frightened to disclose.

I Put Myself on Trial

In a previous post, I wrote about how rigid baby sleep advice contributed to my postpartum mental health crisis. I believed that if I followed the method correctly, Lily would sleep. She didn't.

Instead of questioning the method, though, I questioned myself. Eventually I stopped believing the books, but another problem remained: I didn't believe myself.

My mind became another authority I couldn't escape. If I thought, I hate being a mother, surely that meant I hated motherhood. If I thought, I want my old life back, perhaps having Lily had been a mistake. If I imagined running away, maybe I was secretly the kind of mother who abandoned her child. Every thought became evidence for the prosecution. I wasn't experiencing my thoughts; I was putting myself on trial.

The Cost of Silence

This is what I keep returning to while following the Clancy case. Not whether my experience explains hers; it doesn't. Not whether mental illness excuses violence. That's not my argument.

I keep thinking about the mother sitting somewhere right now with a frightening thought that she hasn't told anyone. Maybe she's afraid she'll be judged, afraid someone will take her baby. Maybe she doesn't understand what's happening inside her mind. Maybe her doctor asks whether she's having troubling thoughts and she says no.

I know something about that woman. I was her.

What if we created more places where mothers could say, I love my baby and I hate this. I want to be here and I want to disappear. I'm scared of what I'm thinking. I need help.

Those sentences should be beginnings. They should not automatically feel like confessions. Some frightening thoughts require urgent intervention. Mine sometimes did. I needed psychiatric care, therapy, medication, hospitalization, a safety plan, and people willing to take my illness seriously.

But taking a thought seriously is different from turning it into a verdict on someone's character. It took me months to understand that distinction.

And one question from treatment began to change everything: Can you live in the in-between for now?

I didn't know it yet, but learning to do that would become the next part of my recovery.

item.title: How to Support Clients With Chronic Illness in Therapy
item.description:
Chronic Illness

How to Support Clients With Chronic Illness in Therapy

7 things I wish every therapist knew about chronic conditions.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Therapy often aims to minimize symptoms, but chronic illness symptoms may not go away.
  • Therapeutic safety requires believing clients with chronic illness about their experiences in their bodies.
  • Acceptance of chronic conditions isn't giving up but a way to move forward that's based in reality.
A Friendly Call, William Merritt Chase, 1895
Source: Public domain

The aim of therapy is often to minimize and reduce—minimize symptoms of depression, anxiety, anger, and other forms of psychological distress, and reduce the impact of harmful behaviors, the recurrence of old relationship patterns, or the grip of unhelpful thoughts. The National Institute of Mental Health describes the goal of therapy as gaining relief from symptoms, maintaining or enhancing daily functioning, and improving quality of life (NIMH, 2024).

We need that energy in the therapy room, especially when clients have been struggling with their mental health in ways that affect their daily functioning.

However, the symptoms of clients with chronic illness and chronic pain may never go away. Their symptoms are, well, chronic. When the emphasis of therapy leans too heavily on symptom reduction, it can induce shame, self-blame, disappointment, and hopelessness—the very feelings keeping people with chronic illness emotionally stuck and struggling.

People with chronic illness need a different type of support in therapy. They need to be believed in their suffering. They need acceptance. They need joy. They need self-trust. They need reassurance. They need to know they’re doing enough and that they’re not to blame for their illness.

The goal of therapy then becomes not to gain relief from symptoms or even to enhance daily functioning, but to improve quality of life even if symptoms never change.

Why I Care About This

I hear stories every week about things therapists have said that caused real harm to clients with chronic health conditions.

These statements aren’t always obvious and loud (e.g., “I don’t believe you want to be healthy.”). More often, individuals with chronic illness tell me these stories of harm with lowered voices, speaking almost in a whisper, with eyes drifting down, as if scared that I too will dismiss them and conclude there was no harm done. Therapists rarely intend to hurt, but without a grounded understanding of life with chronic conditions, many inadvertently reinforce the same ableist, insensitive messages people hear everywhere else (e.g., “A friend of mine was healed by X. Have you tried it?” which reads as, “I don’t trust that you’re doing enough for your body.”)

I’m in a unique position as someone who has been on all sides: the therapist, the patient, and now, the coach. My lived experience with chronic illness and professional expertise has motivated me to put together a list that will support therapists as they support people with chronic illness.

7 Things I Wish Every Therapist Knew About Chronic Illness

  1. Incorporate the body into therapy. Chronic illness is a chronic trauma to the body, and without fostering a connection to the body in therapy, clients may become even more disconnected from their bodies. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy can be helpful at times, but cognitive approaches alone may maintain avoidance of the body.
  2. Don’t offer advice. People with chronic illness are inundated with questions about what they are and are not doing for their health. The questioning creates a false narrative that they’re not doing enough to get better, which then gets internalized.
  3. Set up a flare day contingency plan. A flare is a period when a person's symptoms become more intense or intrusive, sometimes lasting days, weeks, or longer. By planning for flare days in advance, you can create safety in the therapeutic relationship. For example, can the client switch the session to video at the last minute? Do they have a certain number of free passes for late cancellations? Flare day contingency plans value your time and schedule as a therapist, while acknowledging the realities of a client living with an unpredictable condition.
  4. Validate negative thoughts about the body. Sometimes when clients disclose negative thoughts about their bodies and their experience with illness, the thought is based in reality. Such thoughts don’t always need to be reframed or evaluated as true or not true. A simple, “It makes a lot of sense that you feel that way” is incredibly helpful.
  5. Nervous system regulation is important, but dysregulation is understandable. People with chronic conditions have been told they need a regulated nervous system. This knowledge doesn’t make regulation easy or even possible. First, it’s important to offer acceptance and understanding of why a life with illness leads to dysregulation in the first place. Second, while mindfulness skills and grounding exercises are important, they should be used with consent and when the client feels safe enough to pay attention to the body.
  6. Acceptance of chronic illness isn’t defeatist. Acceptance of illness and pain doesn’t mean giving up on symptom improvement. It means acknowledging the reality of the present moment. Acceptance can be the only way out of denial and toward reconnection with the self and body. Psychological flexibility in Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) and distress tolerance in Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) can be useful here.
  7. Chronically ill clients are grieving—a lot. People with chronic illness may be grieving the past they miss, the present that is different than they hoped, and the potential futures they need to give up. Holding space for grief in the therapy room is an important part of supporting clients with chronic illness.

If There’s One Thing That Ties Support for Chronic Illness Together, It’s…

I hope that the list above will help you support clients with chronic health conditions if you’re a therapist or coach, or ask for the support you need if you yourself are seeking therapy for chronic illness.

These tips can help create therapeutic safety because they show an individual with chronic illness that you believe what they are going through. If you remember one thing, remember that believing someone’s experience of their body is one of the most powerful therapeutic interventions.

item.title: Why Losing a Parent Is Hard at Any Age
item.description:
Grief

Why Losing a Parent Is Hard at Any Age

Personal Perspective: Losing a parent, at any age, is anything but simple.

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Grief is a common human experience.
  • Losing a parent, at any age, can be a traumatic loss.
  • Children who lose a parent are at greater risk for negative mental health outcomes.

Grief surprises me. As someone who lost a parent early in life, I have long been the person people turn to when they’re struggling with loss. So, it’s not other people’s grief that surprises me. That makes sense. It’s mine.

Particularly in the past several years, when life has become so full and loss has been pervasive, my feelings of grief about my personal losses have quieted. The anniversary of my father’s death approaches and I need to be reminded to mark it. It is no longer something that I anticipate, but something I need to, awful as it may sound, schedule in to observe. Someone asked me how many years it's been, and both of us were quite stunned to realize 38 years have passed.

Perhaps the biggest difference at this stage of my life is that I am much less alone as a child grieving a parent. Certainly as a young child and then as a teen and young adult, I was different from others because I had lost a parent. At midlife, when the loss of parents becomes more common and expected, I am no longer so different.

What I’ve noticed in the past couple of years is that, embarrassingly, I do not know what to say to people who lose a parent. I should be more clear: I know what to say. I know how to offer comfort, how to ask someone to talk about their parent, what was special about them and what they’ll miss. But it is highly uncomfortable for me. I’m ashamed to admit that I have avoided some interactions with peers who have lost parents because I am struggling with my own feelings so deeply.

After many years of grieving the parent I lost when I was a child, I know how to feel the feelings associated with that kind of death. I know how to brace for the expression on someone’s face when I say that one of my parents died when I was a child. No matter how a parent dies, it is a traumatic loss because parents are supposed to be stable sources of connection for their children. The loss of a parent in childhood upends the sense of stability that is part of the foundation on which children build a world.

What is new for me is the anticipation of losing a parent in adulthood—a parent who I know and who knows me. This is the kind of loss that feels so foreign, so hard to consider, so difficult to approach. As I watch so many go through it, I can see how, even when typical in the course of our lives as humans, this loss can also be traumatic. Even when it happens in the way it is supposed to happen, late in life, expected, planned for, it is still the loss of a parent. It is still the loss of a crucial person in one’s life. Even if the relationship was complicated, this is a different kind of loss than I have experienced.

Research on child bereavement finds that children are at increased risk for the future development of a range of mental and physical health problems due to early loss of a parent. This makes sense, as such a significant adverse childhood experience affects a person wholly and completely. It changes the trajectory of a life. I can know this and still feel that it is somehow just as hard, maybe even harder for some, to lose a parent later in life. The likelihood of developing a mental health condition, an addiction, or a chronic health issue is not going to increase among people who lose parents at midlife…or is it? When we look at these outcomes, do we consider that their development could be connected to the stress of losing a parent, at any age?

article continues after advertisement

As I find myself facing friends who are grieving, I think I can see it, this way that my loss and their losses connect us. It is the shaking of a foundation in a different way. The foundation doesn’t crumble the way it does in childhood, with the stable base disappearing. But it deeply disrupts what’s been built on top of it over the years. As adults, we have created entire lives that began with the foundation set by our parents. If our parents were people we wanted to emulate, that has shaped what has been built. If our parents were people we wanted to escape, that too has influenced who we became.

So to lose a parent, at any age, and to grieve a parent, at any age, is anything but simple, even if it is expected. As I stand by friends as they experience loss and grief, I see them as the children they were, unmoored in the way that I was, even as we have so many years separating our losses.

item.title: What You Should Know About the Lindsay Clancy Case
item.description:
Postpartum Psychosis

What You Should Know About the Lindsay Clancy Case

Understanding medication and treatment resistance and access to life-saving care

Posted August 12, 2026

Key points
  • Postpartum psychosis is a rare but life-threatening psychiatric emergency requiring immediate treatment.
  • Treatment resistance should prompt careful reassessment rather than simply continuing the same approach.
  • Patients and families should always be informed and have access to evidence-based alternatives to treatments.

The heartbreaking deaths of three young children in the Lindsay Clancy case have understandably captured national attention. As testimony unfolds, public conversation has largely centered on one question: Was the mother criminally responsible?

That is an important legal question. But from a clinical perspective, another question deserves equal attention: What can this tragedy teach us about identifying and treating severe psychiatric illness before people reach a point of crisis?

When the Brain Becomes Ill

Severe psychiatric illness can profoundly alter the way a person thinks, perceives reality, and behaves. Intelligence, education, professional success, or even being a loving parent do not make someone immune to serious mental illness. Severe psychiatric disorders are illnesses of the brain—not reflections of intelligence, morality, or character (American Psychiatric Association (APA), 2023). It reflects a brain in crisis.

Society often assumes that people who are educated, successful, or outwardly “high functioning” would somehow be protected from losing touch with reality. Unfortunately, psychiatric illnesses do not discriminate.

Understanding Postpartum Psychosis

The Clancy trial has brought renewed attention to postpartum psychosis, a rare but severe psychiatric emergency affecting approximately one to two women per 1,000 births (Sit et al., 2006; ACOG, 2023). Unlike postpartum depression, postpartum psychosis may involve hallucinations, delusions, profound confusion, insomnia, mood instability, disorganized thinking, and a loss of contact with reality. It requires immediate psychiatric evaluation and, in many cases, hospitalization because the risk of harm to oneself or one’s infant can increase when psychosis is untreated (ACOG, 2023).

Importantly, postpartum psychosis should not become synonymous with violence. The overwhelming majority of women experiencing postpartum depression or other perinatal mood disorders never harm their children or themselves. In fact, sensationalized media coverage may unintentionally increase stigma and discourage mothers from disclosing frightening symptoms out of fear that they will be judged, hospitalized, or lose custody of their children (ACOG, 2023).

article continues after advertisement

When Standard Treatment Isn’t Enough

Another issue highlighted during testimony is one that extends far beyond this individual case: medication- or treatment-resistant depression and psychiatric illness.

Although antidepressants have transformed millions of lives, they are not universally effective. Approximately one-third of individuals with major depressive disorder fail to achieve remission after multiple medication trials, often requiring a reassessment of diagnosis, medication strategy, psychotherapy, or alternative interventions (McAllister-Williams et al., 2020).

Some individuals fail to improve despite multiple medication trials. Others experience intolerable side effects or paradoxical worsening of symptoms. Still others require an entirely different diagnostic formulation or treatment approach. Psychiatry, like the rest of medicine, requires individualized care.

One medication may transform one person’s life while proving ineffective, or even problematic, for another. Rather than assuming a single treatment pathway works for everyone, clinicians must continually reassess when patients are deteriorating or failing to improve.

Expanding the Conversation About Evidence-Based Treatments

One aspect of the current trial has drawn attention to alternative treatment options. Public testimony has indicated that Lindsay raised the possibility of ketamine treatment to her treating psychiatrist. The response she received was that for her to receive insurance coverage for the treatment, she had to fail with four distinct antidepressants. Whether different treatment decisions would have altered the outcome remains unknown and cannot be determined from the available evidence. That question ultimately belongs to the legal process, not speculation.

article continues after advertisement

However, the broader issue deserves serious consideration. Many patients—and even some healthcare providers—remain unaware of evidence-based treatments available for severe, treatment-resistant psychiatric illness. Also, the lack of health care coverage and rigid regulations make it prohibitive for many individuals.

Among alternative treatments are:

Electroconvulsive Therapy (ECT): Despite decades of stigma fueled by inaccurate portrayals in popular culture, modern ECT remains among the most effective treatments for severe depression with psychotic features, catatonia, and treatment-resistant depression. In situations where someone is rapidly deteriorating or suicidal, ECT can produce life-saving improvement much faster than traditional antidepressants (APA, 2021).

Ketamine and Esketamine: Over the past decade, research has demonstrated that ketamine-based therapies can produce rapid reductions in depressive symptoms and suicidal ideation for some individuals with treatment-resistant depression. While not appropriate for every patient and requiring careful psychiatric monitoring, ketamine represents one of the most significant advances in depression treatment in recent years (Alipoor et al., 2001; McIntyre et al., 2021).

Other evidence-based options—including transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), intensive outpatient or partial hospitalization programs, reproductive psychiatry consultation, and multidisciplinary treatment teams may also play important roles depending on the individual’s presentation.

The issue is not that every patient should receive these treatments. The issue is that every patient deserves a comprehensive evaluation of all evidence-based options when conventional treatments are failing.

The Cost of Delay

One of the greatest challenges in mental health care is that deterioration often occurs gradually. Families may normalize worsening symptoms. Patients frequently minimize their distress. Clinicians may interpret changing symptoms through the lens of an earlier diagnosis. Insurance authorization requirements may delay access to specialty treatments.

Each delay may seem small in isolation. Collectively, they can become significant. Mental illnesses evolve. Treatment plans should evolve with them.

A Call for Earlier Intervention

The lessons from this tragedy extend beyond the courtroom.

We need:

  • Greater public education about postpartum psychiatric disorders and broader access to reproductive psychiatrists and specialized mother-baby psychiatric programs where available
  • Insurance systems that allow clinicians to individualize treatment rather than forcing rigid treatment algorithms when someone is rapidly declining
  • Continued research into why some patients develop treatment resistance and how emerging therapies can be integrated safely and effectively
  • To remember that psychiatric illness is fundamentally an illness of the brain
article continues after advertisement

Like heart disease or cancer, early recognition and timely intervention can profoundly influence outcomes.

None of us can know whether different treatment decisions would have changed what happened in this heartbreaking case. Sadly, the family never got the option to find out.

What we can do presently is allow this tragedy to motivate meaningful improvements in education, access to care, early identification, and awareness and access to evidence-based treatment.

Lives can ultimately be saved because clinicians, families, policymakers, insurers, and the public become more aware of severe postpartum psychiatric illness and the full spectrum of available treatments. Maybe some measure of change and hope can emerge from this profound tragedy.
